  3. Choose a trigger that runs after the source value exists. When it depends on submitted answers, this is commonly after validation.
  4. Write the Assignment template using the required fixed value or Liquid expression.
  5. Set the Assign to field ID for the target.
  6. Select the appropriate assignment mode.
  7. Test the source value, target value and every later feature that relies on it.

Use a small, readable template. Put complex transformation logic in an intentional sequence of assignments rather than one long expression that is difficult to diagnose.

Write the assignment template

The Assignment template supplies the value to save. It can be fixed text, a Liquid expression that reads a field, or a structured value where the target expects one.

For example, an action that stores a person’s chosen contact route can use the corresponding field or an earlier action result. Keep the target’s expected format in mind: storing a whole record where a later template expects a single label creates avoidable errors.

Test templates with blank input, optional fields omitted, long text and unexpected characters. A template that works only with ideal data is not ready for a live journey.

Select the target field and mode

Assign to field ID identifies the target. It can address a property within a structured field using dot notation. Only target fields whose meaning and expected shape you understand; a seemingly simple overwrite can destroy a value that another step still needs.

The assignment mode controls how the value is applied:

Mode Use it when Caution
Replace The target should become the new value. It overwrites the previous value.
Append The target is a collection and the new value is another item. Prevent duplicate items if the action can run again.
Merge The target is a structured value and you are updating part of it. Confirm that existing properties are preserved as intended.

If the target is part of a repeating group, use Assign to field iteration to identify the relevant row. The first row is numbered 0. Test more than one row and test adding, removing and reordering rows before relying on an iteration expression.

Keep assignment order explicit

An assignment can consume an earlier action’s result, and a later action can consume the assigned value. Put those actions in that order under the same trigger. Give each a name that describes its hand-off:

  1. find_account
  2. set_account_name
  3. send_account_confirmation

This pattern is easier to test than hiding the transformation inside the sending action. It also lets you inspect each decision point when an external dependency returns incomplete data.

Preserve compatibility deliberately

For new services, use an Assign action rather than placing an action result directly into a result field through older configuration. The explicit assignment records what is being taken from the result and where it is stored.

When maintaining an existing service, do not replace legacy behaviour merely for consistency. First identify the current consumers, reproduce the live behaviour in QA, then make and test a controlled change.

Test checklist

  • The trigger runs only after all source values exist.
  • The template produces the expected value for normal, blank and unexpected input.
  • The target field ID is correct and has the expected format.
  • Replace, append or merge matches the intended data behaviour.
  • Repeating-group assignments have been tested across multiple rows.
  • Actions consuming the target run afterwards.
  • Re-entering a page or resuming a draft does not create unwanted duplicates or overwrite important data.

Related guidance

  • Shared action settings
  • Feed lookup actions
  • Write Liquid templates
  • Group components

articles.title: Delete actions
articles.content:
Use a Delete action to remove previously collected values from the current journey. It is useful when an answer becomes irrelevant, when a person changes direction, or when information should not remain available to later pages and actions.

Deletion is a service-design decision, not just a tidy-up step. Before configuring it, identify every page, condition, document and integration that could use the value afterwards.

Decide exactly what should be cleared

You can clear selected fields or clear all fields associated with one or more pages. Prefer the narrowest scope that meets the requirement.

flowchart TD
  A[Person changes an earlier answer] --> B{Which values are no longer relevant?}
  B --> C[Clear named fields]
  B --> D[Clear fields from a no-longer-relevant page]
  C --> E[Continue with only relevant information]
  D --> E

Clear named fields when only a small number of dependent values must be removed. Clear all fields on a page when the whole page belongs to a route that no longer applies. Do not clear a wider page simply because it contains one outdated answer.

Configure a Delete action

  1. From Page actions, add a Delete action.
  2. Give it a stable ID and an explicit name, for example clear_postal_contact_details.
  3. Choose a trigger that runs after the decision making the data irrelevant has been validated.
  4. Add the field IDs to Delete fields, or select the pages in Delete all fields on pages.
  5. Add execution conditions if deletion should happen only for a particular route.
  6. Test the journey before and after changing the controlling answer.

The action removes answers, not the component definitions. If the person returns to the relevant page later, they can answer the fields again.

Use conditions to protect relevant answers

Pair a Delete action with the same business rule that makes a value irrelevant. For example, when someone changes their preferred contact method from email to telephone, a condition can run an action that clears the email detail only when the new choice is telephone.

Keep the condition positive and readable. A name such as contact_method_is_telephone is easier to audit than a broad inverted condition. Review the action’s trigger and condition together; an action that runs too early can erase information before another action has used it, while one that runs too late can allow obsolete information to be included in a document or message.

Consider repeat visits and drafts

People may go back, revise an answer, leave a draft and return later. Test those behaviour patterns deliberately.

  • Enter values in the fields that might be cleared.
  • Take the route that makes them irrelevant.
  • Continue to the review and completion steps.
  • Go back and choose the original route again.
  • Resume a saved draft and check that the visible fields and stored values agree.

If the service needs an audit of a prior response, do not rely on a delete action. Decide and document where that audit information is retained before designing the route.

Protect downstream actions

An action that sends a message, produces a document or calls another service may depend on data that a Delete action removes. Put prerequisite actions first, and place deletion only after the value is no longer required. Where appropriate, test a document or message after the route changes to make sure it does not display an empty label, stale value or misleading sentence.

Example: clear an alternative address

A service asks whether correspondence should go to a different address. If the person changes Yes to No, a conditional Delete action clears the alternative-address fields after the updated answer has been validated. The review content and completion message then use the main address only.

Test checklist

  • The action clears only the fields or pages that have become irrelevant.
  • Its trigger runs after the decision that justifies deletion.
  • Conditions prevent deletion on routes where the information remains needed.
  • Later actions, documents and review pages do not expect cleared values.
  • Going back, changing an answer and resuming a draft have been tested.
  • The service has an agreed approach where retention or audit information is required.

Related guidance

  • Shared action settings
  • Use conditions and branching
  • Page navigation and journey behaviour
  • Review and completion pages

articles.title: Govforms email actions
articles.content:
Use a Govforms email action to send a configured template-based email from a service. It is suited to confirmations, updates and operational notifications where the email content is managed as a reusable template and the service supplies recipient-specific values.

Configure the email template and its permitted placeholders before linking it to the service. Then add the action from Page actions and choose a trigger that sends only after the relevant answers are complete and valid.

Plan a dependable message

Before configuring the action, confirm the recipient, the template, every variable the template expects, whether attachments are required, and what the service should do if sending fails.

flowchart LR
  A[Validated answers] --> B[Email action]
  B --> C[Resolve recipient and template values]
  C --> D[Send configured template]
  D --> E[Continue to confirmation]

Do not use an email as the only evidence that a service was completed. The completion route should remain clear even if delivery is delayed or a recipient cannot receive messages.

Configure the action

  1. Open Page actions and add a Govforms email action.
  2. Give it a stable ID, for example send_submission_confirmation, and a name that describes when it sends.
  3. Select the email template using its template ID.
  4. Set the recipient email address. You can use a Liquid expression to take it from a field.
  5. Add each template variable key and its matching value.
  6. Add attachments only where the template and the recipient genuinely need them.
  7. Choose a trigger after validation, or on service completion when the message is a final confirmation.
  8. Test with a safe address and representative non-sensitive data in QA.

For more than one recipient, provide one address per line where the service design requires it. Keep the recipient logic narrow and auditable; an unexpected template value should never turn into an unexpected recipient.

Map template variables carefully

Each Template variable key must match a placeholder defined in the selected template. The paired Template variable value can be fixed text or a Liquid expression using information from the service.

Build the mapping as a small table before entering it in Builder:

Template placeholder Service value Example purpose
reference assigned case reference helps the recipient identify the request
name person’s preferred name personalises the message
next_step calculated route instruction explains what happens next

Use clear variable names in the template and keep values in the format the email needs. Test omitted optional answers so the recipient never receives an unexplained blank or raw template expression.

Add attachments with care

Use Attachment variable key and Attachment file together to provide a file to a template variable. Select the uploaded file field or a successfully generated document result as the attachment source.

Attach only files that the recipient needs and is allowed to receive. Confirm the file exists before the email action runs, check that its contents are relevant to the chosen journey, and give the person a clear expectation that an attachment will be sent.

If an email depends on a document-generation action, put document generation first and the email action second under the same trigger. Test the order through the complete route.

Choose timing and conditions

For a message that confirms an answer on the current page, run the action only after page validation. For a final confirmation, use the completion trigger. Apply action execution conditions when only some journeys should send the message, such as an opt-in update or a route requiring an attachment.

Avoid sending on page load unless the page is explicitly designed for that event and repeated visits are safe. A person returning to a page must not unknowingly generate duplicate emails.

Test delivery and content

In QA, test a valid route, a route where the condition skips the action, a missing recipient address, an optional value left blank and an attachment route. Check the rendered email, not only the Builder configuration: subject, recipient, body, substituted values, links and attachment all need review.

Do not put sensitive information in an email just because the service collected it. Use the minimum necessary content and make the person’s expectations about email clear in the journey.

Related guidance

  • Shared action settings
  • Write Liquid templates
  • File components
  • PDF actions
  • Library email configuration

articles.title: Template notification email actions
articles.content:
Use the template notification email action when your organisation has a configured notification provider and the email body is maintained as an approved provider template. The service supplies the recipient and the values that fill the template’s placeholders.

This action is a good choice when content must be consistent across several services or when template changes need to be managed outside the individual service. It is not a substitute for designing a clear confirmation page in the service itself.

Prepare the template before the service action

Create and approve the email template in the configured notification service first. Record its template ID, the exact placeholders it expects, whether it supports attachments, and who owns future changes.

flowchart LR
  A[Approved notification template] --> B[Template ID]
  C[Validated service answers] --> D[Recipient and variable mappings]
  B --> E[Template notification email action]
  D --> E
  E --> F[Recipient receives a completed message]

The service cannot compensate for a template whose placeholders are missing or ambiguous. Give placeholders clear business names such as reference, next_step and contact_name, and keep a simple mapping record with the service.

Configure the action in Builder

  1. Open Page actions, choose Add action, then select the template notification email action.
  2. Set an Action ID and name that identify the event, for example send_decision_email.
  3. Enter the configured Notification template ID.
  4. Set the Email address with a fixed value or Liquid expression.
  5. Add the template variable keys and their matching values.
  6. Add attachment variables only where the approved template expects them.
  7. Select a trigger after validation or at completion, as appropriate.
  8. Test the full delivery route in QA with safe representative data.

The recipient address and template ID are required. Treat both as a dependency: an otherwise correct action cannot send a useful email without them.

Map values precisely

The Template variable key is the placeholder name from the provider template. The matching Template variable value is the service value that should replace it. Values can use Liquid, which is useful for fields and results prepared by earlier actions.

Template variable Example value source Check
reference assigned reference number exists before the action runs
name user-provided preferred name optional value is handled gracefully
next_step calculated instruction makes sense for every route that sends the email

Do not put display formatting, data cleanup and delivery logic into one large template expression. Use a preceding Assign action when a value needs transforming; it makes the email mapping easier to review and test.

Attach documents only when needed

Pair an Attachment variable key with the file or generated document that should fill it. The file must exist before this action runs. If it is generated by a preceding PDF or document action, order the actions so generation completes first.

Check that an attachment is relevant to the selected journey, safe for the recipient, and named clearly. Test the route with no attachment as well as the expected attachment route, so that an optional file does not cause a delivery failure.

Avoid duplicate or premature messages

Use After validation when the email confirms a valid page response. Use the completion trigger when it confirms the finished service. Apply execution conditions for route-specific messages, such as only sending a message when a person opted into updates.

Avoid a page-load trigger unless the page is explicitly designed to send on every visit. People can return to a page, refresh it or resume a draft; the service must not produce an unexpected duplicate message.

Test checklist

  • The template ID identifies the approved email template.
  • Every required template variable has a matching service value.
  • Optional values do not create an unfinished or misleading message.
  • The recipient expression resolves to the intended address for each route.
  • Attachments are produced before the email action and are sent only when relevant.
  • The trigger and conditions prevent duplicate or premature sends.
  • The rendered QA email has been checked, including recipient, content and attachments.

Related guidance

  • Shared action settings
  • Govforms email actions
  • Write Liquid templates
  • PDF actions

articles.title: Template notification SMS actions
articles.content:
Use the template notification SMS action to send a concise, provider-managed text message using information from the service. It is best for short confirmations, reminders or status updates where a person has supplied a valid mobile number and expects contact by text.

Text messages have limited space and are easy to misdirect. Keep them brief, avoid sensitive information, and provide a clear next step without assuming the person can respond.

Decide whether SMS is appropriate

Before adding the action, confirm that the person has chosen or is entitled to receive text messages, the service has a mobile-number field with suitable validation, and the message remains useful without confidential details.

flowchart TD
  A[Valid mobile number] --> B{Permission or relevant route?}
  B -- Yes --> C[Resolve template values]
  C --> D[Send short SMS]
  B -- No --> E[Do not send]

Use email or an in-service confirmation for longer explanations, attachments or information that needs a record people can revisit. An SMS can point to a secure route, but should not contain private form answers.

Configure the action

  1. In Page actions, add the template notification SMS action.
  2. Give it an Action ID and descriptive name, for example send_appointment_reminder.
  3. Enter the configured Notification template ID for the SMS template.
  4. In the recipient setting, supply the mobile number with a field reference or other Liquid expression.
  5. Add each template variable key and its matching value.
  6. Set the trigger and any execution conditions.
  7. Test with an approved QA number and representative, non-sensitive values.

Although the Builder uses the same general recipient and template settings as notification email, the recipient here is a telephone number. Ensure the field and hint clearly ask for a mobile number in the format your organisation supports.

Write for a small screen

Keep template values concise. Long names, references and dynamically generated instructions can make a message hard to read or split across several screen lines. Test with the longest realistic values, not only a short demo record.

Good SMS content usually identifies the service or organisation, states the update, and gives one clear next step. Avoid including a full address, detailed decision, account data or any value that would create a privacy risk if the phone is shared.

Use conditions to respect the route

Attach execution conditions when the message should be sent only for a relevant route. For example, an appointment reminder should run only when an appointment exists and the person has indicated that text contact is acceptable.

Conditions control whether the action runs; they do not validate the mobile number or show a page. Keep validation on the telephone field and use a separate, clearly named condition for consent or route eligibility.

Test timing and delivery

For a response to a submitted answer, send after validation. For a final confirmation, use the service-completion trigger. Avoid page-load triggers for notifications that must be sent only once, because revisiting the page can create additional messages.

Test a valid number, invalid number, blank optional number, route with no permission, changed contact preference and returning to the page. Confirm that the message received is complete, understandable and contains the correct substituted values.

Test checklist

  • The recipient resolves to the intended mobile number.
  • The field collecting the number has clear validation and supporting guidance.
  • The route has a clear, auditable reason to send a text message.
  • Template values are short enough for a readable message.
  • No sensitive information is included in the message.
  • Conditions prevent messages on ineligible routes.
  • Re-entering or resuming the journey does not send unintended duplicates.

Related guidance

  • Shared action settings
  • Text components
  • Use conditions and branching
  • Template notification email actions

articles.title: SES email actions
articles.content:
Use an SES email action when you need to author the subject and body directly in Builder, using a verified sender domain configured for the library. It supports Liquid values, Markdown by default, raw HTML when necessary, multiple recipients and real file attachments.

This action is useful for tailored operational emails. It carries more responsibility than a provider-managed template: the service author owns the clarity, accessibility and safety of the message content.

Prepare the sender identity

The From address domain must be a verified email domain available in the library’s email identities. Configure and verify it before building the action. Set the From address local-part to the part before the @, for example notifications, and optionally add a friendly From display name.

Use a recognisable sender and a working Reply-to address whenever people may reasonably need to respond. Do not use a personal mailbox or an unmonitored address for a service that invites questions.

Configure the email

  1. Open Page actions and add an SES email action.
  2. Set a clear Action ID and name.
  3. Choose the verified sender domain and supply the sender local-part.
  4. Add the display name and reply-to address where appropriate.
  5. Set the recipient in To addresses; add CC or BCC only for a documented business reason.
  6. Write the subject and body, using Liquid values where required.
  7. Add attachments and optional filenames if the message needs them.
  8. Choose a trigger after validation or completion, then test in QA.

Separate multiple addresses with line breaks. Confirm that each recipient is expected to receive the message; CC and BCC are powerful but easy to misuse.

Author the subject and body

The Subject line and Body support Liquid. Use a subject that explains the purpose without exposing sensitive details in notification previews. Keep the body readable in a plain-text context as well as an HTML-capable mail client.

By default, the body is written in Markdown and converted to HTML. Prefer Markdown for headings, lists, links and emphasis; it is easier to maintain and produces a more consistent structure. Turn on Send body as raw HTML only when Markdown cannot express the required content and the HTML has been reviewed for correct, accessible markup.

flowchart LR
  A[Verified sender identity] --> B[Sender and reply-to]
  C[Service values] --> D[Liquid subject and Markdown body]
  B --> E[SES email action]
  D --> E
  F[Optional attachments] --> E
  E --> G[Message delivered]

Do not rely on colour, images or complex tables to communicate essential information. Use descriptive link text and make the action requested of the recipient clear.

Manage recipients and attachments

Use To addresses for people who need to act on or know about the message. Use CC and BCC sparingly, with an approved reason and appropriate privacy consideration. A Liquid expression that can resolve unexpectedly must be tested with blank and unusual inputs.

Choose uploaded file fields or successfully generated document outputs for Attachment field ID. Optionally provide a matching Attachment filename for each attachment; keep names short, meaningful and safe for the recipient. A filename override must align with the corresponding attachment in the same order.

Generate documents before sending the email. Test missing files and a route without attachments so the service handles both deliberately.

Test the final message

Review a delivered QA email on desktop and mobile. Check sender, reply-to, recipient list, subject, Markdown rendering, Liquid substitutions, links, attachment names and the outcome when an optional field is blank. Also test returning to the relevant page to ensure the trigger does not send unintended duplicates.

Important: Keep personal and sensitive information out of subjects, recipient lists and unnecessary copies. An email is not a secure store for the full contents of a service submission.

Related guidance

  • Library settings
  • Shared action settings
  • Write Liquid templates
  • Use Markdown and HTML
  • File components
  • Library email configuration

articles.title: API actions
articles.content:
Use an API action to send a request to an external web service and use its response in the service journey. It can retrieve information, create or update a record, or support a controlled integration with another system.

An API action should be designed with the receiving system’s owner. Agree the endpoint, authentication approach, request and response formats, timeout, error handling, data protection and test environment before adding it to a live service.

Design a safe request and response

Be able to describe the contract in plain language: what information is sent, why, what comes back, and what the person sees if the call cannot be completed.

flowchart LR
  A[Validated service values] --> B[Build request]
  B --> C[External API]
  C --> D{Response received?}
  D -- Expected response --> E[Use result in the journey]
  D -- Timeout or error --> F[Follow designed failure path]

Do not let an external failure leave a person unsure whether their request was recorded. For an essential integration, design a clear retry, review or alternative route. For a non-essential lookup, allow the service to continue only when that is a genuine, safe business outcome.

Configure the action

  1. In Page actions, add an API action and give it a stable ID and clear name.
  2. Choose a trigger after the source values are available and valid.
  3. Set a fixed HTTP method, unless a dynamic method is an explicit integration requirement.
  4. Enter the full URL, including https:// where the endpoint supports it.
  5. Add a request body for methods that send data, then choose its content type.
  6. Add only the headers that the receiving service requires.
  7. Choose the response content type that matches the endpoint.
  8. Set an appropriate timeout, configure client certificates only when required, then test in QA.

Use a fixed method for most integrations. A dynamic method is harder to review and should be used only where the API contract specifically requires it.

Match request and response formats

The request body and Request body content type must agree. A JSON payload should use the JSON content type; a plain-text or form-encoded API needs its corresponding type. A mismatch can make an otherwise valid request unreadable to the receiving system.

Likewise, set Response content type to the format the API actually returns. This tells Builder how to interpret the result for a later template, condition or Assign action. Test a normal success response and each documented error response; APIs do not always return an error in the same format as a success.

Use Liquid only for values that genuinely vary by journey. Escape or format values according to the API contract, especially when placing user-entered text in a JSON body or URL.

Add headers and credentials safely

Enter required Request header names and their paired values in matching order. Keep the number of headers minimal and document why each is needed. Do not place credentials, tokens, private keys or certificate material in action names, descriptions, screenshots or other documentation.

Some organisations require mutual TLS. Turn on the certificate option and supply the required certificate chain, private key and authority chain only through approved secure configuration. Treat certificate rotation as a planned operational activity with a named owner; do not rely on a service author remembering an expiry date informally.

Choose a realistic timeout and prototype response

The request timeout controls how long the service waits before treating the call as unavailable. Start from the integration’s agreed service level. A shorter timeout may provide a faster failure path; a longer timeout may be justified for an operation that the user expects to wait for. Test the user experience around a slow call, not just the successful result.

Use Mock response only for the prototype environment. It lets you exercise templates and routing without contacting the real external system. Keep the mock response representative of the agreed response format, including important optional or error cases. It must not be used as evidence that the production integration works.

Test the integration end to end

Test the request with ordinary, blank, long and unexpected values; review the received request with the API owner; and check how the service uses every expected response. Test each supported HTTP method and content type only where the integration needs it—not as a substitute for a focused acceptance test.

Record the action’s owner, endpoint purpose and failure route in its description or service runbook. An integration that works only because one person remembers how it was set up is difficult to maintain safely.

Related guidance

  • Shared action settings
  • Assign actions
  • Use conditions and branching
  • Write Liquid templates

articles.title: Site upload actions
articles.content:
Use a site upload action to copy files collected by the service, or documents generated during the journey, into the configured file store. It is commonly used to place evidence or a completed document where operational teams can work with it.

Set up the file-store connection at library or service level before adding the action. The action should reference an approved destination and should run only after the required file exists.

Plan the storage journey

Decide which files must be uploaded, where they should be stored, how they will be named, who can access them and what should happen if storage is unavailable.

flowchart LR
  A[Person uploads a file] --> B[File field]
  C[Optional document generation] --> D[Generated document]
  B --> E[Site upload action]
  D --> E
  E --> F[Configured file store]

Do not use an upload action as the only confirmation that a submission was received unless the business process expressly depends on successful file storage. Design a clear failure route when storage is essential.

Configure a site upload action

  1. Confirm that the required file-store connection is configured and available in the target environment.
  2. In Page actions, add a Site upload action.
  3. Give it a stable ID and a name that states the destination purpose, such as store_supporting_evidence.
  4. Choose the appropriate storage provider and configured site or bucket link.
  5. Add each file field or generated document to File.
  6. Supply a corresponding Filename where a specific storage name is required.
  7. Select a trigger after validation or after document generation.
  8. Test the upload and retrieve the stored files in QA.

The service normally inherits its storage arrangement. Select an alternative only when the service requirement and environment configuration support it. Do not improvise a destination by entering an unapproved connection reference.

Choose file sources and filenames

File identifies the upload field or generated document to copy. Add one entry per file. A file must be fully available before the action runs, so document-generation actions must come first.

Filename lets you control the stored name. Where a filename is supplied, keep it meaningful, use a safe extension that matches the file, and avoid putting sensitive information into the name. Ensure every filename entry aligns with its file entry in the same order.

File source Suitable filename approach
Evidence uploaded by a person keep the original name when appropriate, or apply a controlled case reference
Generated review document use a clear reference and document type
Several supporting files retain a predictable order and unique names

Use a stable reference rather than a person’s full name where a file may be visible to operational teams who do not need that information.

Respect environments and access

The QA and production environments can use different destinations. Test both deliberately; a successful QA upload does not prove the production connection, permissions or folder structure are correct. Verify who can open the stored file and whether they can distinguish test data from real submissions.

Before go-live, check retention, deletion and access requirements with the storage owner. The upload action moves a file—it does not decide your organisation’s retention policy.

Handle failure and repeat visits

Test a missing file, a rejected upload, an unavailable storage connection and a person returning to the page. If a retry can create duplicate copies, decide whether duplicates are acceptable or whether the journey needs an explicit recovery route.

Keep downstream email and completion actions in the right order. If a message says a document was stored, the upload must complete first; if a message only confirms submission, do not imply that the storage operation succeeded without checking its outcome.

Test checklist

  • Each source file exists before the action runs.
  • The storage provider and destination are approved for the service and environment.
  • Every filename aligns with the intended file and does not reveal unnecessary information.
  • Multiple files upload in the expected order with distinguishable names.
  • QA and production destinations have been tested separately.
  • A failed or repeated upload has a deliberate operational response.
  • Stored files can be opened by the intended team and are not accessible more widely than required.

Related guidance

  • File components
  • Shared action settings
  • SharePoint site link settings
  • Service files, email and integrations
  • Library cloud storage connections

articles.title: List add actions
articles.content:
Use a list add action to create a new item in a configured SharePoint list, or to add-or-update an item when a matching record already exists. It is suitable for handing a structured service result to a team that works from a list.

Configure the site connection and both QA and production lists before creating the action. Treat the list schema as an integration contract: changing a column name or type without reviewing the action can break the service.

Choose between adding and adding-or-updating

Choose Add a new item when every completion should become a distinct list item. Choose Add or update when the service should maintain one item for a known business key, such as a case reference.

flowchart TD
  A[Validated service values] --> B{Write mode}
  B -- Add new item --> C[Create a list item]
  B -- Add or update --> D[Run matching list lookup]
  D -- Match --> E[Update existing item]
  D -- No match --> C

Add-or-update requires a separate list lookup action that finds the existing item. Put the lookup before the list add action, use the lookup’s Action ID in Site Lookup Action, and test both match and no-match routes. Without a reliable unique key, add-or-update can overwrite the wrong item.

Configure the destination

  1. Select the configured SharePoint site connection.
  2. Choose the intended List to work with in the QA environment.
  3. Choose the corresponding List to work with in the Production environment.
  4. Confirm the lists have matching business columns and data types.
  5. Add the column mapping.

Keep QA and production separate. Test data must never be written to the operational list, and a QA success does not prove that the production list permissions and columns are correct.

Map columns to service values

For each value, select the QA and production column names, enter the Column value, and choose the corresponding Column data type. The visible Column name is useful for maintainers; use it to describe the business purpose of the mapping.

List column purpose Suitable service value Type check
Case reference assigned or entered reference text
Received date calculated date date-compatible value expected by the list
Priority flag condition or choice result boolean
Supporting link approved URL hyperlink object where required

Values can use Liquid. Keep formatting and transformation explicit: use an Assign action first when the list needs a computed value. For each mapping, confirm that blank optional answers, long text and choice values remain valid for the target column.

Use Indexed columns only where the list owner has designed and approved indexes. Indexes can improve queries, but they are not a substitute for an effective business key or sensible list design.

Order the actions safely

Place a list lookup before an add-or-update action. Place any Assign actions that prepare values before the list write. Put a redirect last, after the list operation and any required confirmation work.

Choose a trigger after the page has validated if the mapped values come from that page. For a final operational hand-off, the service-completion trigger may be more appropriate. Avoid a page-load trigger for a write action unless repeated visits are deliberately safe; a return to the page could create duplicate items.

Test the operational outcome

In QA, check the list item itself rather than stopping at a successful journey. Confirm the correct columns, values, types, link shape and destination. Test a missing optional value, a duplicate key, an edited journey and the add-or-update match/no-match cases.

Agree with the list owner how errors are monitored and resolved. A failed write should lead to a defined operational process, not an invisible gap between the service and the team receiving the work.

Test checklist

  • QA and production use the intended, separate list destinations.
  • Each mapped column exists and has the expected data type in both environments.
  • Liquid values and optional fields produce valid list values.
  • Add a new item and add-or-update are chosen for the correct business need.
  • Add-or-update has a reliable preceding lookup and unique key.
  • Revisiting a page cannot create accidental duplicate items.
  • QA tests verify the written list item, not only the service page.

Related guidance

  • List lookup actions
  • SharePoint site link settings
  • Shared action settings
  • Assign actions

articles.title: List lookup actions
articles.content:
Use a list lookup action to retrieve one or more items from a configured SharePoint list. It can support a search page, find an existing item before an add-or-update operation, or bring a controlled list value into the journey.

Keep lookup rules narrow and explainable. A list search that returns unexpected matches can make a person see the wrong information or cause a later action to update the wrong record.

Set up the connection and result shape

Select the configured SharePoint site and the matching QA and production lists. Then decide whether the action should return one result, multiple results, or a single value from one column.

flowchart LR
  A[Search value or earlier result] --> B[List lookup rules]
  B --> C{Results}
  C -- One intended item --> D[Use or update item]
  C -- Several items --> E[Present or process the result set]
  C -- No items --> F[Show the designed no-match route]

Choose Single result only where the rules identify one record. Choose Multiple results when the service is designed to handle a set of records, for example a search result table. Use Limit results to column when a later action requires only a single column value rather than the full record.

Add matching rules

Data feed elements define the comparisons used to filter the list. Match a field, earlier action result or controlled value to the relevant list column. Use exact matching for identifiers; use partial or fuzzy matching only for a deliberate search experience with clear user guidance.

When there are several rules, use all of them when each must pass—such as matching both a reference and a status. Use any of them only when either rule is intentionally enough. Test changed letter case, leading spaces, blank values and duplicate records, as these are common causes of misleading results.

Use a custom OData filter expression only when the standard rule configuration cannot express the required query. It overrides the configured rules, so record why it is needed, have it reviewed by the list owner, and test it with realistic values. A custom query is powerful but harder for a future service author to maintain.

Control large result sets

For a rich or large list, configure paging deliberately. A fresh lookup starts a new result set; next, previous and current modes are used with the action’s paging information to navigate it. The page size can be from 1 to 1000 items.

Start with the smallest page size that supports the user task. Smaller pages reduce the amount of data processed at once and make a results screen easier to understand. Test first, next, previous and final pages, plus a search that returns no records.

Do not request a large result set simply because the list has many items. Improve filtering before increasing the page size.

Use lookup results safely

An action result can be used by a component, condition, template or a following list add action. Give the action an ID that describes its purpose, such as find_existing_case, and ensure consumers run after it.

For an add-or-update flow, configure the list lookup first and reference its Action ID from the list add action. The lookup needs a dependable business key; broad lookup rules should never decide which record to update.

Design an explicit no-match outcome. It might offer another search, direct the person to enter a new record, or route the case to a team. Do not silently continue with empty data.

Test checklist

  • QA and production point to the intended, separate lists.
  • Rules match the correct columns using the appropriate comparison type.
  • The selected result mode reflects the business expectation.
  • The no-match, duplicate and unexpectedly broad-result paths are designed and tested.
  • Custom OData is justified, reviewed and tested independently.
  • Paging works across first, next, previous and final result pages.
  • An add-or-update action uses this lookup only with a reliable unique key.

Related guidance

  • List add actions
  • Results table components
  • Shared action settings
  • SharePoint site link settings

articles.title: PDF actions
articles.content:
Use a PDF action to generate a portable document from the service’s review content. It is useful when a person, reviewer or downstream process needs a fixed version of the answers after they have been collected.

Create the PDF only when the answers are ready for that purpose. A document generated too early can omit later answers or capture a route that the person subsequently changes.

Choose where the PDF belongs in the journey

Common patterns include generating a PDF on a review page, on completion, or immediately before an email or file-upload action that needs the document.

flowchart LR
  A[Answers are validated] --> B[Review content is ready]
  B --> C[PDF action]
  C --> D[Download, attach or store PDF]

Name the action for the document’s purpose, such as generate_submission_record or create_review_copy. If another action needs the PDF, put that action after PDF generation under the same trigger.

Configure the action

  1. Open Page actions on the page where the document should be created.
  2. Add a PDF action.
  3. Set a stable Action ID and an understandable name.
  4. Choose a trigger after the relevant answers have been validated or when the service is complete.
  5. Enable digital signing only where signing is configured for the target environment and the business process requires it.
  6. Test the generated document in QA with normal, long and optional answers.

The action uses the service’s review content. Check the review-page headings, labels and any conditional content before treating the PDF as an official record.

Use digital signing deliberately

The Digitally sign PDF setting applies the platform’s configured digital signature when signing is enabled for the environment. Turning it on does not by itself provide a signing service, approval process or evidence of a person’s intent. Confirm the legal and operational requirement with the responsible team before relying on it.

Test signed and unsigned behaviour in the intended environment. Ensure recipients know what the signature indicates and how they should validate it. If the environment does not have signing enabled, the output remains unsigned.

Design a readable document

Use clear component labels and review-page structure, because these become the basis of the PDF. Long free text, repeated group rows, optional answers and conditional routes need particular attention.

Review the generated file visually at ordinary zoom and in a PDF reader. Check that headings are clear, long answers are not confusing, page breaks do not separate labels from values unnecessarily, and content that was not relevant is not shown as an unexplained blank.

Avoid adding sensitive information to a review page just to get it into a PDF. Include only what the intended recipient needs.

Use the PDF in later actions

A generated PDF can be used as the source for a later email attachment or file upload. Use the action’s result only after successful generation, and test a failure route where document creation is unavailable.

For a document that must be retained, pair generation with the approved storage action and confirm that the stored filename and permissions meet the operational requirement. Do not rely on the person’s browser download as the only retained copy where an organisational record is required.

Test checklist

  • The trigger creates the PDF only when the intended answers are complete.
  • Review content and conditional routes are correct before generation.
  • Long, optional and repeated answers remain readable in the output.
  • Any email or file upload runs after the PDF action.
  • Digital signing is enabled only for an approved, configured process.
  • The QA document has been opened and checked visually, not only generated successfully.

Related guidance

  • Review and completion pages
  • PDF review components
  • Site upload actions
  • Govforms email actions

articles.title: Templated PDF actions
articles.content:
Use a templated PDF action when a service must fill an existing PDF layout: for example, a regulated form, a partner document or a carefully designed printable record. The action overlays text or marks onto positioned boxes in an uploaded PDF template.

This is a precision feature. Build and test the template with the document owner, because a small change to the source PDF can shift every mapped value.

Prepare a stable template

Use a final, approved PDF template with a clear version and owner. Upload it through the templated PDF action settings; Builder records the template used by the action. Avoid replacing a live template without reviewing every mapping and generating a comparison document in QA.

flowchart LR
  A[Approved PDF template] --> B[Upload template]
  C[Service fields and Liquid values] --> D[Mapping boxes]
  B --> E[Templated PDF action]
  D --> E
  E --> F[Filled PDF for review or storage]

Keep the source file’s page order and dimensions stable. A new template version should be treated as a controlled change, even if it appears visually similar.

Configure the action

  1. Add a Templated PDF action from Page actions.
  2. Set a stable Action ID and a descriptive name.
  3. Upload the approved PDF template and confirm its displayed filename.
  4. Add one mapping box for each answer or mark that should appear on the PDF.
  5. Choose the trigger after all mapped values are available.
  6. Enable digital signing only for an approved, configured signing process.
  7. Generate and inspect QA documents with representative answers.

The stored template reference is managed by Builder. Work through the template upload controls rather than attempting to set an internal file reference yourself.

Map text and marks

Each mapping has a stable Mapping ID, a page number and a box position. Page numbering begins at 0, so the first PDF page is page 0. The X and Y coordinates, width and height are proportions of the page, from 0 to 1.

Use a Text mapping for a field value, a selected part of a multi-part field, or a Liquid value. Use a Mark mapping for a selection, with a tick, cross, filled shape, circle or strikethrough as appropriate.

Mapping choice Use it for Important check
Field ID a direct answer from the service the field exists on every route that produces the document
Field part one part of an address, date, time or location only the intended part appears
Value template calculated or combined content blank and unexpected values render safely
Choice ID + mark marking a selected option the mark appears only for the intended selection

Make mapping IDs meaningful, such as applicant_name_page1 or consent_tick. They help maintainers trace each box back to its purpose.

Fit content into the document

Set font, alignment and vertical alignment to suit the allocated box. A single-line answer often works best with bottom alignment; longer text generally needs top alignment. Use a sensible font size and minimum font size, but do not depend on shrinking to make an unsuitable answer fit.

Test the longest realistic answer, including names, addresses and free text. If text becomes too small to read, redesign the question, restrict the input or use a different document layout. Do not solve a layout issue by silently reducing important information to illegible text.

Set Read only for boxes that must not be edited during PDF review when editing is enabled. Use it sparingly and make sure the person can still correct the original service answer where needed.

Test every layout route

Generate PDFs for each conditional route, each choice that creates a mark, a blank optional value, long text and a repeated-group answer where relevant. Inspect every page at normal zoom. Check that values do not overlap labels, marks do not appear in the wrong box, and page-specific mappings stay on the correct page.

When the template changes, repeat the whole mapping check. Do not assume a coordinate that worked in the prior version is still correct.

Related guidance

  • PDF actions
  • PDF review components
  • Write Liquid templates
  • Site upload actions

articles.title: HTML actions
articles.content:
Use an HTML action to generate an HTML representation of the service’s review content for a later action or integration. It is useful where a downstream system needs structured rendered content rather than a PDF.

An HTML action does not create a new public web page. Treat its output as data for a controlled downstream use, and decide who will receive it and how it will be handled before configuring the action.

Choose the output mode

The action offers two output shapes:

Output mode Use it when Includes
Full document the recipient needs the complete rendered document context outer document structure and associated presentation material
Main content only a downstream system needs the lightweight review-content fragment the main review content without the full outer document

Choose the smallest output that meets the integration’s need. A lightweight fragment is often easier to send or embed; a full document is useful only when the consumer expects complete rendered-document context.

flowchart LR
  A[Review content ready] --> B[HTML action]
  B --> C{Output mode}
  C -- Full document --> D[Complete rendered document]
  C -- Main content only --> E[Lightweight content fragment]
  D --> F[Controlled downstream use]
  E --> F

Configure and use the output

  1. Add an HTML action from Page actions.
  2. Set a stable Action ID and name that describe the output consumer.
  3. Choose the trigger after the review content and values are ready.
  4. Select the full-document or main-content-only mode.
  5. Place the later action that consumes the output after this action.
  6. Test the full downstream hand-off in QA.

If the generated HTML is sent to another system, agree how that system will handle styles, scripts, links and user-entered text. Do not assume that HTML which looks correct in one context will be safe or readable in another.

Review the content, not just the response

Test a normal route, optional answers omitted, long free text and every conditional section. Inspect the generated output in the same way the receiving system will use it. A successful action response only proves that content was generated; it does not prove the consumer renders it safely or correctly.

Use clean review-page content: meaningful headings, clear labels and no instructions that are relevant only while completing the service. This produces more useful HTML for documents, emails or integrations.

Avoid including sensitive values unless the downstream use has been approved. The HTML can contain the same personal information as the review content, so its retention and access rules must be considered alongside the receiving system.

Related guidance

  • Review and completion pages
  • PDF actions
  • Shared action settings
  • Use Markdown and HTML

articles.title: Redirect actions
articles.content:
Use a Redirect action to send a person to another page, reload the current page, move them back one page, or direct them to an external URL. Redirects are powerful journey controls: use them only when normal page navigation and conditions cannot express the intended route clearly.

Always place a redirect last among actions sharing the same trigger. Once navigation begins, a later action may not run.

Choose the redirect type

Redirect type Use it when Consideration
Internal the target is a known page in the same service use the selected page’s stable Builder reference
Internal dynamic a Liquid expression deliberately chooses an internal target test every possible resolved target
External the person must continue at an approved external URL they leave the service; make this explicit
Reload current page the page needs to refresh after a controlled action avoid loops and repeated work
Go back one the journey must return to the preceding page test the effect on saved answers and history 
flowchart TD
  A[Page action runs] --> B{Redirect type}
  B -- Internal --> C[Another page in this service]
  B -- External --> D[Approved external destination]
  B -- Reload --> E[Current page refreshed]
  B -- Back one --> F[Previous page]

Use an ordinary page condition rather than a redirect when the requirement is simply “skip this page when the answer does not apply”. Conditions keep the flow easier to see and maintain.

Configure an internal redirect

  1. Add a Redirect action from Page actions.
  2. Give it a clear ID and name, such as send_to_payment_step.
  3. Choose Internal and select the target page.
  4. Add execution conditions if the redirect applies only to a particular route.
  5. Decide whether the person should be able to go back to the redirected-from page.
  6. Put the redirect after every prerequisite action.
  7. Test forward navigation, browser back behaviour and a resumed draft.

The target must be a valid page in the service. Normal flow restrictions still apply, so a redirect is not a way to bypass pages that the journey design prevents a person from reaching.

Use external redirects carefully

An External URL can use Liquid and must begin with http:// or https://. Use only a controlled, approved destination. Clearly tell the person that they are leaving the service, especially if the next site has a different sign-in, privacy notice or support route.

Do not construct an external URL directly from unreviewed user input. If a value needs to affect the destination, constrain it to a known set and test every result. Confirm that service data is saved at the intended point before the person is redirected.

Use a Redirect fragment only when the target supports a specific, useful anchor. Avoid fragments as a substitute for clear page structure.

Manage back history and transient values

The redirect settings can remove the current page, or all pages since the target, from the person’s back history. Use this only when returning to those pages would create an invalid, confusing or unsafe route. Preserve history by default so people can review and correct answers.

The setting to prevent clearing values on page load should be used only when you understand the page’s transient behaviour. Test the route after reload, back navigation and draft resumption; retaining a value that should reset can be as harmful as clearing a value that the next action needs.

Add query parameters only when required

You can attach paired Query parameter name and Query parameter value entries to the redirect. Use these for a documented integration need, not for carrying sensitive information. Parameters can be visible in browser history, logs and referral data.

Keep names and values aligned in the same order. Test how the target receives them, including blank optional values and URL encoding.

Test checklist

  • The normal page flow or a condition cannot express the route more simply.
  • The action is last in its trigger sequence.
  • Internal targets are valid and every dynamic target has been tested.
  • External destinations are approved, clear to the person and use safe input.
  • Back-history behaviour matches the journey design.
  • Reload and back-one routes do not loop or repeat important actions.
  • Query parameters are necessary and contain no sensitive information.
  • Browser back and resumed drafts work as intended.

Related guidance

  • Page navigation and journey behaviour
  • Use conditions and branching
  • Shared action settings

articles.title: Review actions
articles.content:
Use a Review action to pause a service for one or more reviewers to accept, return or cancel it. It creates a deliberate approval step: reviewers receive an invitation, see the approved review information and choose from the actions you allow.

Design the review process with the operational team before configuring it. Agree who may review, what they can see, how many approvals are needed, what happens when work is returned, and who handles stalled or cancelled reviews.

Design the approval route

The review name is visible in the journey and can appear in a task list. Write it as a clear status, such as “Manager approval” or “Quality check”, rather than a technical action name.

flowchart TD
  A[Service information is ready] --> B[Review action]
  B --> C[Invite reviewer or reviewers]
  C --> D{Reviewer decision}
  D -- Accept --> E[Continue approval route]
  D -- Return --> F[Person updates and resubmits]
  D -- Cancel --> G[End or route for follow-up]

Choose the action’s trigger after all information a reviewer needs is ready. Do not start review before required validation, document generation or essential checks have happened.

Configure a review

  1. Add a Review action from Page actions or the appropriate workflow step.
  2. Set a stable Action ID and a plain-language Review name.
  3. Specify the reviewer invitation recipients and, if useful, matching recipient names.
  4. Choose how many reviewers must accept: one, a specified number, or all reviewers.
  5. Decide exactly which fields reviewers need to see.
  6. Set the permitted reviewer actions and make the button labels describe their outcome.
  7. Add instructions and notification content.
  8. Test accept, return and cancel with representative reviewer accounts in QA.

For multiple reviewers, make the approval threshold explicit. “Any one”, “two reviewers” and “all reviewers” lead to materially different operational outcomes; test them with the actual number of invitees.

Show only the information needed

By default, a review can show all fields. Limit the display to selected fields when reviewers do not need the full submission. This is often the better choice for privacy, faster decisions and clearer reviewer screens.

Use Fields to show the reviewer to select the relevant information, and optionally show page titles so reviewers understand the context. Review the resulting screen from the reviewer’s perspective, not only the service author’s perspective.

Do not include sensitive information simply because it was collected. If a reviewer needs a derived result rather than raw data, use a preceding Assign action or a short review instruction instead.

Write instructions and controls

Additional review data text content appears with the review information. Use it for concise decision guidance, policy references and the evidence a reviewer should consider. Review actions intro text content appears before the decision controls; use it to explain what accepting, returning or cancelling will do.

Write the content in Markdown unless raw HTML is genuinely necessary. Keep the instructions useful without turning the review screen into a manual. Use clear headings and short lists for longer checks.

Reviewers can be allowed to:

Action Meaning Use it when
Accept approve and continue the route the reviewer can make the decision
Return send the work back with comments the person can correct or clarify it
Cancel stop the review route a controlled termination is required

Custom button text should describe the consequence. For example, “Approve request” is clearer than “Continue” when approval is the reviewer’s decision.

Handle returned work carefully

Decide whether a returned service must have a changed answer before it can be resubmitted. Requiring a change can prevent an unchanged loop; allowing resubmission without a change may be appropriate where a reviewer’s comment was informational or an external issue has been resolved.

Test the whole return route: reviewer comment, user notification, reopened information, corrected answer, resubmission and renewed invitation. Confirm that the reviewer can identify what changed where the process needs that context.

Configure notifications deliberately

The review action can send invitations, acceptance, return and cancellation notifications through the configured email method, or not send a notification for a particular event. Map recipients, templates and variables separately for each stage; a correct invitation does not prove the return or cancellation message is configured.

Use reviewer email expressions that resolve to the intended people. If you supply names, keep them in the same order as the email addresses. Keep notification content brief and avoid including sensitive submission details in messages or subjects.

For template-based notifications, check every template ID, variable and attachment mapping. For direct email notifications, review sender, recipient and reply-to behaviour. Test the delivered messages in QA for accept, return and cancel outcomes.

Operate the review process

Name an owner for delayed reviews, failed notifications and reviewer access problems. A review action creates a workflow state; it does not replace an operational process for clearing a queue or escalating overdue work.

Document the expected service-level time, reviewer group, decision criteria and escalation route alongside the service. Review those details whenever the organisation changes roles, policy or notification templates.

Test checklist

  • The review starts only after all required information is available.
  • The review name and task-list status are understandable to the person.
  • Reviewers see only the fields they need.
  • Approval threshold matches the intended policy and number of reviewers.
  • Accept, return and cancel actions have clear labels and tested outcomes.
  • The returned route allows or requires changes according to the agreed process.
  • Invitation, acceptance, return and cancellation notifications each work in QA.
  • Delays, failed delivery and reviewer access have an operational owner.

Related guidance

  • Shared action settings
  • Task list services
  • Review and completion pages
  • Write Liquid templates

articles.title: Add to cart actions
articles.content:
Use an Add to cart action to store one or more related items in a named cart while a person completes a service. It can support a basket-style journey, a collection of selected products, or a structured set of choices that later actions need to process together.

Treat a cart as journey data, not as a payment or stock-management system. If the service has financial, inventory or legal consequences, connect it to the appropriate controlled downstream process.

Design the cart structure first

Decide the cart’s purpose, the stable name for it, the stable identifier for each item, and the data each item needs to retain. A clear structure prevents one page from accidentally replacing information added by another.

flowchart LR
  A[Person selects or configures an item] --> B[Add to cart action]
  B --> C[Named cart]
  C --> D[Review cart content]
  D --> E[Submit, process or amend]

Use one cart per distinct collection. For example, keep selected_services separate from supporting_documents. Do not reuse a cart ID for unrelated data just because the items are added on the same page.

Configure an Add to cart action

  1. Add an Add to cart action from Page actions.
  2. Give the action a stable ID and name that describe what it adds.
  3. Set the Cart ID to the stable collection name.
  4. Set the Cart item ID to a stable key for the selected item or items.
  5. Use Cart item value to store the information later steps need.
  6. Turn on Merge with existing only when a later page intentionally contributes extra properties to the same item.
  7. Choose a trigger after the relevant answers have validated, then test adding, changing and revisiting items.

Cart IDs, item IDs and values support Liquid. Use a clear preceding Assign action if an item needs a complex calculated value; this makes the cart action easier to read and maintain.

Use stable item IDs and useful values

The Cart item ID is the key used to identify an item within its cart. It can represent a single item or a collection of items. Make it stable and meaningful, such as standard_subscription or a controlled catalogue identifier. Do not use a label that may change for editorial reasons.

The Cart item value holds the data for the item. It can be a simple value or a structured object. Store only the values that later pages or actions need, and avoid duplicating sensitive fields that already exist elsewhere in the journey.

Element Good practice
Cart ID a stable collection name, for example selected_products
Item ID a unique business identifier, not display text
Item value concise, predictable data needed by review or processing
Action name describes the business event, for example “Add selected product”

Understand merge behaviour

With Merge with existing turned off, adding the same item ID replaces the existing item value. With merge turned on, the new object’s top-level properties are combined with the existing item instead.

Use merge only when multiple, controlled steps contribute different parts of the same item. It is a shallow merge: do not assume it will intelligently combine deeply nested data. Test the resulting value when properties overlap, when one page omits an optional property and when a person returns to edit an earlier page.

Prevent duplicates and stale selections

An action may run again when people revisit a page, resume a draft or retry a route. Design the item ID and trigger so that repeated execution does not create accidental duplicates or silently overwrite important data. Use a Remove from cart action when an item should disappear after a person changes their selection.

Make the cart visible in a review or summary step where appropriate. A person should be able to understand what they have selected and amend it before the service commits a consequential outcome.

Test checklist

  • The cart ID represents one clear collection.
  • Every item ID is stable and unique within the cart.
  • Values contain only the information later steps need.
  • Replace and merge behaviour matches the intended route.
  • Revisiting or resuming a page does not create duplicate or stale items.
  • Changing a selection removes or updates the earlier item deliberately.
  • The review or processing step uses the expected final cart content.

Related guidance

  • Remove from cart actions
  • Shared action settings
  • Assign actions
  • Review and completion pages

articles.title: Remove from cart actions
articles.content:
Use a Remove from cart action to remove one or more items from a named cart, or to clear the entire cart. It is essential when a person changes a previous selection and the service must not retain an item that is no longer relevant.

Configure removal with the same care as adding: an incorrect cart or item ID can remove a valid selection, while a missing removal action can leave stale data for review or downstream processing.

Choose the removal scope

Set the Cart ID to the collection you want to change. Then either identify the item or items to remove, or leave the item setting blank only when the whole cart must be cleared.

flowchart TD
  A[Person changes a selection] --> B{What is no longer relevant?}
  B -- One or more items --> C[Remove matching item IDs]
  B -- Entire collection --> D[Clear the named cart]
  C --> E[Review updated cart]
  D --> E

Prefer removing named items. Clear a full cart only when the entire collection has genuinely become invalid, such as restarting a selection stage.

Configure a removal action

  1. Add a Remove from cart action from Page actions.
  2. Give it a stable ID and a specific name, such as remove_unselected_product.
  3. Set the Cart ID.
  4. Add the Cart item ID or IDs to remove.
  5. Leave the item ID empty only for an intentional full-cart clear.
  6. Apply an execution condition that represents the change of route.
  7. Choose a trigger after the controlling answer has validated.
  8. Test changing the selection, returning to the page and resuming a draft.

The item ID supports Liquid, so it can be calculated from an answer or a preceding action. Keep dynamic item IDs constrained to known values and test a blank result before deploying.

Pair removal with the controlling decision

Use a condition that clearly states why the item should go. For example, when a person changes from “Add an additional service” to “No”, a condition can run the removal action for the additional-service item.

Do not use a broad cleanup action that clears data whenever a page loads. That can remove valid choices when someone returns to review or edit a different part of the journey.

Check downstream dependencies

Review pages, pricing logic, documents and external actions may use cart content. Put the removal action before any later action that reads the updated cart. Test the complete route so no document, email or external submission includes an item the person removed.

If an item has already been sent to an external system, removing it from the cart does not necessarily cancel it outside the service. Design a separate cancellation or amendment process for external consequences.

Test checklist

  • The action targets the intended cart.
  • Named item IDs remove only the intended item or items.
  • A blank item ID is used only for an intentional full-cart clear.
  • The removal condition reflects the business rule that makes the item irrelevant.
  • Revisiting or resuming the journey does not clear valid items.
  • Review, documents and later actions use the updated cart content.
  • External effects have a separate cancellation process where required.

Related guidance

  • Add to cart actions
  • Use conditions and branching
  • Delete actions
  • Shared action settings

articles.title: Fetch form actions
articles.content:
Use a Fetch form action to retrieve a submission from the same organisation for use in the current service. It can retrieve a specific submission, the latest completed submission for a user, or the latest completed submission for a group.

This action can expose personal or operational information across journeys. Start with the smallest data scope and the normal access restriction. Expand access only after a documented privacy, security and business review.

Decide what must be fetched

Choose the lookup basis that matches the business need:

Fetch by Use it when
Submission ID the service has a specific submission reference to retrieve
User ID the latest completed submission for the same user is needed
Group ID the latest completed submission for a permitted group is needed

Choose No fields when only submission metadata is required, Selected fields when the current route needs a small known set of values, or All fields only where the full context is genuinely needed. Selected fields are usually safer and easier to maintain.

flowchart LR
  A[Current service has a permitted reference] --> B[Fetch form action]
  B --> C{Access and filter checks}
  C -- Allowed --> D[Return minimum required data]
  C -- Not allowed or no match --> E[Follow clear alternate route]

Configure the action

  1. Add a Fetch form action from Page actions.
  2. Set a stable Action ID and a name that identifies the purpose, such as retrieve_previous_application.
  3. Select Fetch by and supply the corresponding submission, user or group template.
  4. Set the target service if it differs from the current service.
  5. Choose the smallest appropriate field scope.
  6. For selected fields, list the exact field IDs or permitted context values to return.
  7. Add a filter field and value where the retrieved submission needs an additional business check.
  8. Keep the normal access scope unless a formal approval authorises broader access.
  9. Test allowed, denied, no-match and incorrectly scoped requests in QA.

Use field selection and filtering

Use Selected fields to return only the values that a later page or action needs. This reduces unnecessary data exposure and makes it clear which fields the current service relies on. When field names change, review the fetch action alongside the affected service.

An optional Filter field and Filter field value adds an extra match requirement in the target service. Use it to enforce a known relationship, such as a case reference or organisation identifier. It is not a replacement for access control; it is an additional business check.

Do not fetch all fields because it is convenient during development. That can expose values to templates and actions that do not need them and makes privacy review much harder.

Keep access scope narrow

By default, the action can retrieve only submissions the current runtime user may already access. This is the correct setting for most services.

The broader Access scope option can allow access to any user’s submission in the organisation. Use it only where there is a clear, approved role and process that needs it. Document the reason, restrict which values are fetched, provide an audit route, and test with accounts that should and should not have access.

Important: A valid submission ID is not, by itself, permission to show someone’s data. Keep the normal access restriction unless the organisation has explicitly approved a wider scope.

Handle no match and stale data

The latest completed submission may not be the one a person expects, and a supplied reference can be missing or stale. Design a no-match route that tells the person what they can do next without revealing whether another person’s submission exists.

Test what happens when the target submission is incomplete, closed, changed, belongs to a different user or group, or contains an optional selected field that is blank. Review any content that displays fetched data to ensure it remains accurate and understandable.

Test checklist

  • The fetch basis matches the business relationship between services.
  • The target service and filters identify the intended submission.
  • The action returns the minimum field set needed.
  • Default access restrictions remain in place unless wider access is formally approved.
  • No-match and denied-access paths are clear and do not disclose sensitive information.
  • Field IDs, optional values and changed target submissions have been tested.
  • QA tests use accounts with both permitted and non-permitted access.

Related guidance

  • Set form status actions
  • Authorization actions
  • Shared action settings
  • Write Liquid templates

articles.title: Set form status actions
articles.content:
Use a Set form status action to reopen or close a specific submission in the same organisation. Reopening makes the target submission editable and incomplete; closing marks it complete and closed.

Changing another submission’s status can alter someone’s ability to work on it. Use this action only as part of a clearly designed workflow with an agreed owner, audit process and recovery path.

Choose the status change carefully

Target status Effect Typical use
Open reopens the target submission for editing returning work for correction or resumption
Closed marks the target submission complete and closed completing a controlled workflow step 
flowchart LR
  A[Approved workflow decision] --> B[Identify exact submission]
  B --> C[Set form status action]
  C --> D{New status}
  D -- Open --> E[Submission can be edited]
  D -- Closed --> F[Submission is complete and closed]

Do not use this action as a general substitute for validation or a review decision. The action changes state; it does not explain the business reason to the person affected.

Configure the action

  1. Add a Set form status action from Page actions or the owning workflow step.
  2. Set a stable Action ID and a name that describes the business event, such as reopen_for_correction.
  3. Set the Submission ID template to the exact submission to change.
  4. Specify a target service only when it differs from the current one.
  5. Choose Open or Closed.
  6. Keep the normal access scope unless a formally approved role needs wider authority.
  7. Add execution conditions so the action runs only for the intended decision.
  8. Test the changed submission with an appropriate QA user.
